0.title: Hopes for This Life, and the Living Hope
0.essay:
Everyone lives by hope. The student hopes to pass, the couple hope for a child, the patient hopes the scan is clear, the nation hopes for better leaders. Take hope away and something in us begins to die. The question is never whether we will hope, but what we will hope in, and whether it can bear the weight.

An age of small hopes

Our culture is full of hopes, and strangely short of hope. We have more comfort than any generation before us, yet many people, especially the young, look at the future with dread. What is left is often a private hope: that my own life will turn out well, for as long as it lasts.

A hope that does not put us to shame

The Bible speaks of a different kind of hope. It is not a mood, and not wishful thinking. It is a settled expectation of what God has promised, resting on what he has already done in Jesus Christ. Peter says that God “has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). Paul says that this hope “does not put us to shame” (Romans 5:5). It will not let us down.

This study looks at what that hope is, where it comes from, what it waits for, and how it changes an ordinary Monday, and asks how to hope for good things in this world and keep hoping when the answer is “not yet”. The studies Death, Dying & Heaven, Disappointment & Waiting, Christian Suffering and Already and Not Yet sit close by.

The chapters

We Cannot Live Without Hope; What Hope Is; The Hopes That Disappoint; The God of Hope; Born Again to a Living Hope; What We Are Waiting For; Hoping in This World; Hope in the Dark; When Hope Is Deferred; Hope That Changes Today; A Reason for the Hope; and Christ Our Hope.

For reflection

What are you hoping for at the moment, large or small? If someone asked you what your deepest hope rests on, what would you say?

1.title: We Cannot Live Without Hope
1.essay:
Human beings live forwards. We get up in the morning because something is ahead of us: a meal, a meeting, a holiday, a grandchild’s visit, a day off. We are made to lean into the future. That is why the loss of hope is one of the heaviest things a person can carry.

Hope gets us out of bed

Most of our hopes are small and ordinary, and that is good. But beneath them lie larger ones: that our lives will matter, that we will be loved, that our children will be safe, that wrongs will one day be put right. We hardly notice these hopes until they are threatened. Then we discover how much they were holding us up.

What despair does

Scripture is honest about the absence of hope. Job, sitting in the ashes, says, “My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle and come to their end without hope” (Job 7:6). He even looks at a felled tree with envy: “For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again” (Job 14:7), but a man “breathes his last, and where is he?” (Job 14:10). The writer of Lamentations, looking at the ruins of Jerusalem, says, “My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD” (Lamentations 3:18).

These words are in the Bible. God does not hide from us that believers can come to the edge of despair. Neither Job nor Lamentations ends there. But for a while, the lights went out.

What Frankl saw

Viktor Frankl was a Jewish psychiatrist from Vienna who survived Auschwitz and other Nazi camps. In Man’s Search for Meaning he described how prisoners who lost all sense of a future, of something or someone still waiting for them, often gave up and declined quickly. He tells of a fellow prisoner who had dreamed that the camp would be freed on a particular date in March. As the day came and nothing changed, the man fell ill and died within days. Frankl also reports that the camp doctor noticed a sharp rise in deaths between Christmas 1944 and the New Year, which he put down to prisoners who had hoped to be home by Christmas and lost heart when they were not.

Frankl was not writing as a Christian. But he saw something true about how God has made us. Hope is not a luxury. It is close to the centre of what keeps a human being alive.

Eternity in the heart

Why are we like this? The Preacher says that God “has put eternity into man’s heart” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). We cannot help asking whether anything lasts, and whether our story ends well. Augustine, at the start of his Confessions, said in effect that God made us for himself and our hearts stay restless until they rest in him. Our hunger for hope is a homing instinct. Every smaller hope is, in the end, a pointer to the one hope we were made for.

That is a warning: if we ask small things to carry the weight of that eternal longing, they will buckle. It is also an invitation, because the God who placed the longing in us has not left it empty. He has given a hope that reaches past death itself, and he has given it in his Son.

If you are near despair

Some who read this are not thinking about hope in the abstract. You may feel that there is no way forward at all. If you have any thought of ending your life, please do not wait: tell someone today. Call the emergency services or a crisis line, or go to a trusted person and say the words out loud. That is not weakness.

For a longer struggle with hopelessness, speak to your pastor and ask for a biblical counsellor, through your church or an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the United States or Biblical Counselling UK. A good counsellor will ask you to see your doctor as well, because body and soul affect each other. Medical treatment is no failure of faith. And the counsellor will open God’s Word with you, which is sufficient for the care of the soul. The study Depression & the Christian says more.

An example

A man in his sixties retires after forty years in one firm. For the first month he enjoys the freedom. By the third month he is sleeping late, not shaving, and snapping at his wife. “There’s nothing to get up for,” he tells a friend from church, who invites him to help with a weekly breakfast for homeless men, and to read the Psalms with him on Thursday mornings. Slowly he discovers that his life was never held up by his job, but by God, who still has work and a future for him.

For reflection

What larger hopes lie underneath your everyday plans? Have you known a time when hope drained away? What helped? Why do you think God put “eternity” into the human heart? Is there someone you know who needs you to sit with them in the dark this week?

2.title: What Hope Is
2.essay:
“I hope it doesn’t rain tomorrow.” In everyday speech, hope means a wish with a shrug. We would like something to happen, but we have no idea whether it will. The Bible uses the word very differently. Biblical hope is not a wish. It is a certainty that has not yet arrived.

Three parts of hope

Paul gives the shape of it: “For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25).

Hope, then, has three parts. It looks to something good, something worth waiting for. It looks to something future, not yet seen: once it arrives, we no longer hope for it, we enjoy it. And it looks to something sure, because the waiting is patient, not anxious. You do not wait patiently for a bus that may never come. You wait patiently for a train that is on its way.

Hope and faith

Hebrews brings faith and hope together: “Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Faith and hope are twins. Faith takes hold of what God has said. Hope leans forward to what God has promised. John Calvin put it simply: hope is nothing other than the expectation of the things that faith has believed God has truly promised. Faith says, “God has spoken.” Hope says, “So it will come.”

This means Christian hope is never a matter of temperament. Some people are naturally sunny and some are naturally gloomy. Biblical hope is open to both, because it does not come from looking inward at our mood or outward at our circumstances. It comes from looking up at God’s promise. A cheerful person can have no hope at all, and a person of melancholy temperament can be anchored in hope through the darkest week.

An anchor behind the curtain

Hebrews 6 explains why the hope is sure. When God made his promise to Abraham, “he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:17–18). God’s word would have been enough. He added an oath, not because he needed to, but because we did. He stooped to our weakness and swore.

Then comes the famous picture: “We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf” (Hebrews 6:19–20).

An anchor is fixed somewhere other than the ship. That is the whole point of it. If it were fastened to the deck, it would be useless. Our hope is not fastened to our feelings or our circumstances. It is fastened in heaven itself, in the very presence of God, “behind the curtain” where the high priest once went only once a year with blood. And it is fastened there by a Person. Jesus has gone in “as a forerunner”, one who runs ahead so that others will follow. He is not in heaven merely as our example. He is there “on our behalf”. Where he has gone, we are going. Our hope is as secure as his place at the Father’s right hand.

Faith, hope and love

Paul says, “So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13). Hope is one of the three great marks of the Christian. Elsewhere Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians’ “steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 1:3), and tells believers to wear “for a helmet the hope of salvation” (1 Thessalonians 5:8). A helmet guards the head. Hope guards the mind against the blows of fear, discouragement and despair.

An example

A young mother, a new Christian, admits to her small group that she is “not a hopeful person”. She worries about everything and expects the worst. Someone gently points out that biblical hope is not a personality type. The group reads Hebrews 6 together. She writes “anchored behind the curtain” on a card and puts it on her fridge. She still worries. But she begins to notice the difference between how she feels and what is true, and to let the second speak louder.

For reflection

How is biblical hope different from the everyday “I hope so”? Why does it matter that our anchor is fixed outside ourselves? What does it mean to you that Jesus has gone ahead “as a forerunner on our behalf”? Where do you need the “helmet” of hope this week?

3.title: The Hopes That Disappoint
3.essay:
Most of the things people hope in are good things. Money, family, health, success, a strong economy, a better government. The trouble is not that they are bad. The trouble is that they cannot hold the full weight of a human heart. When a good thing becomes our ultimate hope, it will sooner or later let us down.

Do not trust in princes

Psalm 146 is blunt: “Put not your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation. When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish” (Psalm 146:3–4). Leaders, however gifted, are mortal. Their plans die with them, and sometimes before them. Then the psalm turns: “Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 146:5–6).

David says the same about military power: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7). Chariots and horses were the high technology of the day. Every age has its own.

The shrub and the tree

Jeremiah gives two pictures. “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD. He is like a shrub in the desert” (Jeremiah 17:5–6). It survives, but it never flourishes. “Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD. He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes” (Jeremiah 17:7–8).

Notice that the tree still faces heat and drought. Hope in God does not exempt us from hard years. But the roots go down to water that does not dry up. The shrub depends on the rain; the tree has a stream.

Our own idols of hope

What are the princes and chariots of our time? For some, it is money: the pension, the house, the savings that will make us safe. Paul tells the rich not to “set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). For others, it is a person: the spouse or child who must make us happy, and who buckles under the pressure. For many, it is politics: elections are treated almost as days of salvation or damnation.

The study Idols of the Heart explores how good things become gods. Here the point is simpler. Anything you hope in, other than God, can be lost, and one day will be.

The hope of progress

There is one more hope worth naming, because it shaped the modern world. For two centuries much of the West believed in progress: that science, education and reason would steadily make humanity better and the world kinder. Medicine and technology have brought great blessings. But the twentieth century, with its world wars and death camps, shook the belief badly, and today many expect the future to be worse.

Timothy Keller often pointed out that the West’s confidence that history is heading somewhere good was borrowed from the Bible, and that when the God of the Bible was set aside, the hope was kept but its foundation was removed. A hope without a foundation does not last long. That is part of why our age swings between bright optimism and dark dread.

Good things in their place

None of this means Christians should despise money, family, work or politics. They are gifts, and we will see in a later chapter that it is right to hope for good things in this life. The question is where they sit. When God is our hope, everything else can be enjoyed without being worshipped, and lost without our being destroyed. The psalmist says, “And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you” (Psalm 39:7).

An example

A woman in her fifties had poured her life into her son. When he moves abroad and rarely calls, she feels as though the floor has gone. In tears she tells her pastor, “He was everything to me.” Over months, with prayer and the Psalms, she learns to love her son as a gift rather than lean on him as a saviour. Strangely, their phone calls become warmer once he no longer has to carry her whole life.

For reflection

Which good things are you most tempted to make your ultimate hope? How would you react if you lost them? What is the difference between the shrub in the desert and the tree by the stream in your own life? How does Psalm 146 shape the way you think about elections and leaders?

4.title: The God of Hope
4.essay:
A promise is only as good as the person who makes it. Christian hope is sure for one reason only: it rests on God, who never lies, never changes, never forgets and never fails.

The God of hope

Paul ends his long argument in Romans with a prayer: “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope” (Romans 15:13). He calls God “the God of hope”. Hope is not something we generate and then bring to God. It comes from him. He is its source, its object and its guarantee.

Hope is the Spirit’s work. We do not abound in hope by trying harder to feel positive, but as the Spirit fills us “in believing”. And just before this prayer, Paul tells us how he usually works: “whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15:4). Hope grows where the Bible is read.

Hope against hope

Paul’s great example is Abraham. God promised him descendants as many as the stars. Abraham was about a hundred, and Sarah had never been able to have children. Every human hope was gone. “In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, ‘So shall your offspring be’” (Romans 4:18).

That phrase is worth slowing down for. Against every natural hope, Abraham hoped in God. And Paul is careful to say that this was not denial: “He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb” (Romans 4:19). He looked the facts full in the face. Then he looked past them to God: “No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised” (Romans 4:20–21).

Abraham was not perfect, as Genesis shows. But at the deepest level his hope rested on who God is, “the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17). And in time, “the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised” (Genesis 21:1).

Why God can be trusted

Scripture gives us reason after reason. God is truthful: Paul speaks of “eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began” (Titus 1:2). God is faithful: “Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful” (Hebrews 10:23). God is powerful: Paul learned in a near-death crisis to rely “not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9). And God is loving, beyond any doubt, because of the cross: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

That last verse is the deepest ground of all. If you ever doubt that God means good towards you, look at what he has already given. The hardest thing, the costliest thing, the giving of his beloved Son, is already done. Everything else he has promised is small beside it. “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Hope that looks the facts in the face

This is what makes Christian hope different from optimism. Optimism looks at circumstances and decides they will probably turn out well. Hope looks at God and knows that he will do what he has said, however the circumstances look. Optimism needs good news. Hope can live on God’s word alone. That is why Christians can face a hard diagnosis or a wayward child without pretending, and without despair.

An example

A couple in their late thirties have been told that the business they built is likely to fold. They spend an evening writing down, honestly, everything that is wrong. Then, on the other side of the page, they write down what God has promised: his presence, his provision, his good purpose, his love shown at the cross. The list of problems does not shrink. But they go to bed praying, and wake up able to face the bank manager. The business closes six months later. Their hope does not.

For reflection

What does it mean to call God “the God of hope”? How did Abraham face the facts and still hope? Which of God’s qualities do you most need to remember this week? How does Romans 8:32 answer your fears about the future?

5.title: Born Again to a Living Hope
5.essay:
Most hopes are fragile. They can be crushed by a letter, a phone call, a test result. Peter speaks of a hope that cannot be killed, because it is joined to someone who has already gone through death and come out the other side.

A living hope

Peter begins his first letter with an outburst of praise: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3).

He was writing to suffering Christians scattered across what is now Turkey. The first thing he tells them is not how to cope, but what God has done. They have been “born again” by his mercy, and that new life is born into hope.

Why does Peter call it a living hope? Because it is alive with the life of the risen Christ. A dead hope is one whose object is gone: the job that will never come back, the person who has died. Peter had known a dead hope. On the Friday his Master was crucified, his hope went into the tomb. On the Sunday it walked out again. Christian hope is living because Christ is living, and because “Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again” (Romans 6:9), the hope that rests on him cannot die either.

An inheritance kept for you

Peter goes on: we are born again “to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you, who by God’s power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time” (1 Peter 1:4–5).

Every earthly inheritance is exposed to three dangers. It can perish, wasting away like a house left empty. It can be defiled, spoiled by quarrels and greed. It can fade, losing its value over time. The inheritance God keeps for his children is safe from all three. And there is a double guard. The inheritance is “kept in heaven for you”, and you are “being guarded” for it. God guards the treasure, and God guards the heir. Neither can be lost.

If Christ has not been raised

Paul makes the same point from the other side. Some in Corinth doubted the resurrection of the dead. Paul says that if there is no resurrection, then Christ has not been raised, and everything collapses: “And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins. Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied” (1 Corinthians 15:17–19).

That is remarkably honest. Paul does not say Christianity is useful even if untrue. Christian hope stands or falls on a fact of history.

“But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Earlier in the chapter Paul lists the witnesses: Peter, the twelve, “more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive” (1 Corinthians 15:6), James, all the apostles, and finally Paul himself. He is inviting the Corinthians to go and ask. The study Apologetics sets out the evidence more fully.

The firstfruits

“Firstfruits” is a harvest word. The first sheaf of the harvest was brought to God as a sign and pledge that the whole harvest was coming. Christ’s resurrection is not a one-off miracle. It is the first sheaf of a vast harvest. What happened to his body in the garden tomb will happen to the bodies of all who belong to him. His rising is our rising begun.

On that first Easter morning the angel said, “He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him” (Mark 16:6). Here is the wonder of it: the Son of God went down into our death so that our death would become a doorway, and he came back out holding the keys.

An example

A woman in her forties sits at her father’s funeral. He trusted Christ for fifty years. As the coffin is lowered, she grips the order of service, on which the minister has printed 1 Peter 1:3. She weeps. Yet she finds herself thinking: this is not the end of his story, because it was not the end of Jesus’ story. Months later, she says that the word “living” in that verse is what carried her through the first year.

For reflection

What makes Christian hope “living” rather than dead? Why does Peter mention both the inheritance being kept and believers being guarded? How does 1 Corinthians 15:17–19 show that Christian hope rests on a fact? What difference does it make to call Christ’s resurrection the “firstfruits”?

6.title: What We Are Waiting For
6.essay:
Ask many people what Christians hope for, and they will say “going to heaven when you die”. That is true as far as it goes, and it is a great comfort. But the Bible’s hope is larger. It looks to the day when Christ returns, the dead are raised, and heaven and earth are made new. And at the centre of it all is not a place but a Person.

Not the end of the world

The study Death, Dying & Heaven looks closely at death and the new creation. Here we gather the main lines of the hope.

Paul says that “the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19). The whole created world, “subjected to futility” because of human sin, is waiting “in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:20–21). The world is not heading for the scrap heap. It is heading for liberation. Peter says, “according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13).

Bodies raised

We are waiting too. “We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). Christians do not hope to escape from bodies into a vague spiritual existence. We hope for bodies made new. “We await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:20–21).

Think of what that means for the person with dementia, the child born with a disability, the body worn out by cancer. None of these is the last word. The God who made the body will remake it.

No more tears

John sees the end of the story: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth … And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, ‘Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away’” (Revelation 21:1–4).

Every grief we have known, every injustice, every hospital corridor and graveside, will be gone. Not forgotten as though it never mattered, but wiped away by the hand of God himself.

They will see his face

But the heart of the hope is not the absence of pain. It is the presence of God. In the city John sees “no temple … for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). The whole city is lit by God’s glory, “and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23). And then the line that takes the breath away: “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4).

Moses was told that no one could see God’s face and live. Now the redeemed will look on it for ever. John says elsewhere, “we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). David had longed for this: “One thing have I asked of the LORD … to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD” (Psalm 27:4).

That is heaven. Not harps and clouds, but home: the face of the Father, the Lamb who was slain at the centre of the throne, the Spirit filling all things, and every one of God’s people gathered in. On that day the redeemed will say what Isaiah foresaw: “Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us” (Isaiah 25:9). Every longing for beauty, love, justice and home will find what it was reaching for.

Why this matters now

A hope this solid changes today. A believer with a failing body can say with Paul that “this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

An example

A man whose wife has advanced multiple sclerosis reads Revelation 21 to her every Sunday evening. She can no longer speak clearly, but she squeezes his hand at “no more tears”. He says that this is not escapism. It is the only thing that makes sense of their love: they were made for more than this, and they are going there together.

For reflection

How is the Bible’s hope larger than “going to heaven when we die”? What difference does the resurrection of the body make to the way you see your own body, or someone you love? What does it mean to you that “they will see his face”? Which line of Revelation 21–22 do you most need to hold on to?

7.title: Hoping in This World
7.essay:
If our final hope is the new creation, is it wrong to hope for things now? May a Christian hope to marry, to have children, to recover from illness, to get the job, to see their nation flourish? The Bible’s answer is yes. But it teaches us to hold these hopes in a particular way.

Build houses and plant gardens

When Judah was carried into exile in Babylon, false prophets promised a quick return. Jeremiah wrote: “Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters … But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare” (Jeremiah 29:5–7).

God told his people, far from home, to invest in ordinary life and the good of a pagan city. Their final hope did not make them passive. It freed them to hope and work for good things where they were.

This is the setting of a much-loved verse: “For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope” (Jeremiah 29:11). It is often read as a promise that my plans will succeed soon. In fact it came with a warning that the exile would last “seventy years” (Jeremiah 29:10). Many who first heard it would die in Babylon. The promise was true, but on God’s timescale and for his people as a whole. That is a deeper comfort, not a lesser one.

If the Lord wills

James warns those who plan to “trade and make a profit” as if the future were theirs: “yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes” (James 4:13–14). Instead we should say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15).

James does not forbid planning or profit. He forbids planning as though we were in charge. “If the Lord wills” turns our hopes into prayers, and holds them with an open hand.

Two kinds of hope

So there is a difference between our earthly hopes and our final hope. Earthly hopes are good, but uncertain. We may pray for healing and not receive it, hope for marriage and stay single, work for a cause and see it fail. God has not promised every particular good thing in this life. Our final hope is certain, because God has promised it in Christ and raised him from the dead.

If we treat earthly hopes as certain, we will feel betrayed by God when they fail. If we despise them, we become cold and passive. The answer is to hope freely, pray boldly, work hard, and hold it all loosely, because our life does not depend on it.

Will the world get better?

Christians have disagreed about how much to expect for the world before Christ returns. Postmillennial believers, including many Puritans and Jonathan Edwards, expect the gospel to spread until most of the world is converted, bringing a long age of peace and righteousness before Christ comes. They point to promises such as Isaiah 11:9. Premillennial believers expect things to grow darker until Christ returns and reigns on earth. Amillennial believers see the present age as Christ’s reign from heaven, with the gospel advancing and opposition continuing side by side until the end. The study End Times Models sets these out fully.

This commentary’s view: Scripture promises that the gospel will run through every nation and that Christ’s kingdom will grow like a mustard seed, so we may labour with real hope of fruit. But it does not promise steady improvement of the world before he returns; it speaks of wheat and weeds growing together until the harvest. Our hope for the world rests finally on his coming, not on our progress. That keeps us from both naive optimism and cynical despair, and sends us to seek the welfare of our cities with patience.

An example

A single woman in her thirties longs to marry. For years she has felt guilty about wanting it so much. Her pastor reads Jeremiah 29 and James 4 with her, and she realises she is free to hope, pray and take sensible steps, as long as she holds the hope open to God. She writes in her journal: “If the Lord wills.” Some weeks it is a prayer of trust, some weeks a cry. Both, she discovers, are faith.

For reflection

Which earthly hopes are you carrying at the moment? Are you holding them as certainties or as prayers? How does the setting of Jeremiah 29:11 change the way you read it? What would it look like for you to “seek the welfare” of your town this year?

8.title: Hope in the Dark
8.essay:
Hope is easy to talk about on a sunny day. The real test comes in the hospital ward, the empty house after a funeral, the sleepless night. The Bible does not offer a hope that only works in good weather. It shows us people hoping with tears on their faces.

Arguing with your own soul

Psalms 42 and 43 were written by someone far from the temple, mocked by enemies, sinking under grief. “My tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all the day long, ‘Where is your God?’” (Psalm 42:3). He feels it as a flood: “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Psalm 42:7).

Three times he speaks to himself: “Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God” (Psalm 42:11). He names his feelings, but refuses to let them have the last word. He talks back to his own soul. The study Depression & the Christian looks closely at these psalms; here notice simply what hope does. It does not pretend the pain is small. It reminds the soul of something bigger.

This is the heart of biblical lament. Lament is not the opposite of hope. It is hope refusing to let go of God. To cry out “Why have you forgotten me?” (Psalm 42:9) is still to speak to God. The person who laments has not given up on him. The study Christian Suffering explores lament more fully.

But this I call to mind

Lamentations was written in the ruins of Jerusalem. The writer has said, “my hope from the LORD” has perished (Lamentations 3:18). Then he turns: “But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness. ‘The LORD is my portion,’ says my soul, ‘therefore I will hope in him’” (Lamentations 3:21–24).

Notice what brings hope back. Not a change of circumstances: the city is still in ruins. He calls something to mind. Hope returns through remembering who God is. That is why Christians in the dark need truth in front of them: a verse on the wall, a psalm read aloud, a hymn sung by friends when they cannot sing.

Suffering that produces hope

Paul makes a startling claim: “we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:3–5).

We would expect suffering to destroy hope. In believers, God uses it to deepen hope. Suffering strips away false hopes. Endurance forms a tested character. And tested people learn that God is real in the dark. It is a hope that “does not put us to shame”: it will not leave us embarrassed on the last day for having trusted.

And the ground of it all is love: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts.” Paul goes straight on to say where that love was shown: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). The Son of God entered the darkness, even the darkness of being forsaken on the cross, so that no believer’s darkness would be without him. He has been further into the night than any of us, and he came out the other side.

When the dark is very deep

Some suffering brings a person to the edge. If you are thinking of ending your life, please tell someone today: call the emergency services or a crisis line, or go to someone you trust. For longer struggles, ask your church to connect you with a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to see your doctor. Medical help is no failure of faith. God’s Word is sufficient for the soul, and he often carries us through the hands of others.

An example

A father whose teenage son has died cannot pray for weeks. Each Sunday two friends from church sit with him. One of them reads Lamentations 3:21–24 aloud. At first the father says nothing. One evening, months later, he says the words with them: “his mercies never come to an end.” He tells them he does not feel it yet. But he has started to call it to mind.

For reflection

How does the writer of Psalm 42 speak to his own soul? What could you “call to mind” on your hardest days? Have you seen suffering produce hope, in your life or someone else’s? Who do you know who needs friends to hold hope for them right now?

9.title: When Hope Is Deferred
9.essay:
Some hopes are not crushed in a moment. They are simply postponed, again and again. The prayer is prayed for years. The child is still far from God. The healing does not come. The Bible has a phrase for this slow ache, and it is one of the most honest lines in Scripture.

Hope deferred

“Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life” (Proverbs 13:12). The wise man does not scold the sick heart. He describes it. Waiting wears us down, body and soul. If you feel heavy after years of unanswered prayer, Scripture is not surprised.

The psalmists knew it too: “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1). Yet that same short psalm ends, “But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation” (Psalm 13:5). The circumstances have not changed between verse 1 and verse 5. The man has turned his face again towards God. The study Disappointment & Waiting walks slowly through these long seasons; here we look at how they fit into the bigger story of hope.

They died in faith

Hebrews 11 is often called the hall of faith. It is also a hall of waiting. After Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Sarah, the writer says, “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13).

Abraham was promised a land and owned only a burial plot. He died waiting. So did Joseph, who at the end of his life “made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones” (Hebrews 11:22). He was so sure of God’s word that he arranged for his bones to be carried to the promised land.

Yet these people are not presented as failures. “They desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16). Their hope was not mistaken. It was larger than they could see.

Something better

The chapter ends with a remarkable line: “And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect” (Hebrews 11:39–40).

God was not slow. He was gathering a bigger family, including people like us. When we wait, we too are part of a story we cannot fully see. Peter says, “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9). Even the delay of Christ’s return is mercy.

The one who waited for us

We do not wait alone. Simeon spent his life “waiting for the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25), and at last held the infant Christ in his arms. And Christ himself knew what it was to wait for joy: he “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). He knows the long middle of the story. Now he “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25) for those who are still waiting.

How to wait

Some practical help. Keep praying honestly. Tell God how long it has been. That is what Psalm 13 does. Keep a record of God’s faithfulness in other areas, so that the deferred hope does not blot out everything else. Let others share the load. Tell one or two trusted friends what you are waiting for, so they can pray with you. Hold the earthly hope open, and the final hope fast. And if the ache turns to despair, seek help quickly, from your church and, where needed, a biblical counsellor and your doctor.

An example

A woman has prayed for her husband’s conversion for twenty-two years. One day she reads Hebrews 11:13 and weeps: perhaps she too will die “not having received”. But she also reads verse 16, that God “is not ashamed to be called their God”. She decides that whether or not she sees the answer, she will keep greeting it “from afar”. Her husband is still not a believer. But he has started asking why she is so peaceful.

For reflection

Which of your hopes has been deferred the longest? How does it help to know that Scripture calls this a “sick” heart, not a faithless one? What does Hebrews 11:39–40 teach about God’s timing? How might you “greet from afar” a promise you may not see fulfilled in this life?

10.title: Hope That Changes Today
10.essay:
Some people imagine that thinking about the future life makes Christians useless in this one. The opposite is true. The Bible’s hope does not lift us out of the present. It reaches back into Monday morning and changes how we work, spend, love and face danger.

Hope makes us pure

John writes, “Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure” (1 John 3:2–3).

A bride preparing for her wedding does not need to be nagged to get ready. Her hope does it. Christians fight sin not to earn a future with Christ, but because that future is secured and we long to be fit for it.

Grace that trains us

Paul ties grace, hope and holiness together: “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (Titus 2:11–14).

Grace has appeared in the past, when Christ came and died. Glory will appear when he returns. We live “in the present age” between the two appearings, trained by the first and drawn by the second.

Not in vain

After his long chapter on the resurrection, Paul draws a very practical conclusion: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Because Christ is risen, nothing done for him is wasted: the Sunday school lesson to six children, the meal taken to a neighbour, the care of an elderly parent. That frees us from the need to see results now. It also gives courage. The Hebrew Christians “joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one” (Hebrews 10:34). People who are sure of their future can afford to lose things today.

Hope makes us generous

Paul tells the rich to be “generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future” (1 Timothy 6:18–19). If the best is still to come, we do not need to squeeze everything out of this life.

C. S. Lewis, in his chapter on hope in Mere Christianity, observed that the Christians who did most for this present world were often those who thought most about the next. Heaven made them useful on earth.

Feeding hope day by day

Hope, like a fire, needs fuel. Here are some ways to feed it.

Begin the day with a promise. Before the phone, read one promise of God and say it back to him. The Psalms are full of them.

Say “if the Lord wills” as you plan. It turns plans into prayers and keeps your hopes in the right order.

Keep the Lord’s Day. Gathering with God’s people is a weekly rehearsal of the future. At the Lord’s Supper we “proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26).

Remember the dead in Christ. Visit a grave, or thank God for a believer who has died, and say aloud, “We will see them again.”

Pray the Bible’s last prayer. “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

An example

A nurse on a busy ward feels she is pouring herself into a bucket with holes. Patients leave, new ones arrive, nothing seems to last. A friend points her to 1 Corinthians 15:58. She begins praying on the drive to work, “Lord, today my labour is not in vain in you.” The ward is no easier. But she finds she can be kinder to the difficult patient and more patient with the new staff, because she is no longer working for results she can see.

For reflection

How does the hope of seeing Christ make a believer want to be pure? Where do you need to hear that your labour “is not in vain”? How might hope make you more generous this month? Which of the habits above could you start this week?

11.title: A Reason for the Hope
11.essay:
In a hopeful culture, Christian hope might pass unnoticed. In an anxious one, it stands out. When people around us are afraid of the future, a believer who is calm, kind and steady will sooner or later be asked a question: why?

Always be prepared

Peter writes to Christians facing hostility: “Have no fear of them, nor be troubled, but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:14–15).

Peter assumes that Christian hope will be visible, in how we face illness, loss, persecution and the news, and that people will want to know where it comes from.

Notice too the order. First “in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy.” A reason for hope begins with a heart that is set on Christ. Then “always being prepared”: Christians should think about how to explain their hope, simply and honestly. And then “with gentleness and respect”. We are not winning arguments. We are offering bread to hungry people.

Without hope and without God

Paul reminds the Ephesian Christians what they were before Christ: “separated from Christ … having no hope and without God in the world” (Ephesians 2:12). The two go together. Without God, there is no final hope. There may be many plans and much cheerfulness, but no ground for believing that the story ends well.

Our age often feels this keenly. Many young people expect the world to be worse in their lifetime; some decide not to have children for fear of the future. Many thoughtful secular people seek meaning in kindness and the beauty of the world, and some live admirably. But they admit that, on their view, the universe is not going anywhere, and every human life will in the end be forgotten.

Into that world, Christians bring news, not just advice. “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). God has acted. Christ has died and risen. There is a future, and it has a face.

How to give a reason

Some practical help for ordinary conversations.

Ask what people hope for. “What are you looking forward to?” or “What keeps you going?” are gentle questions that open real conversations. Listen well before you speak.

Tell your own story. When did hope become real to you? What has it meant in a hard time? Personal honesty often reaches further than a list of arguments.

Point to the resurrection. Christian hope is not a nice idea but rests on an event. Be ready to say why you believe Jesus rose. The study Apologetics can help.

Do not hide your struggles. Christian hope is not pretending everything is fine. When people see that you grieve, but “not … as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13), they see something real.

Be gentle and respectful. Treat people as image-bearers of God, not projects. The study Evangelism says more about understanding people and sharing the gospel.

Hope as witness

In the early centuries, Christians were noticed for how they cared for the sick in times of plague and faced death with courage. Today hope may be seen in a hospital bed, a redundancy, a funeral, or simply in a person who is not crushed by the news. A hopeful Christian in a hopeless age is itself a question waiting to be asked.

An example

A man in his twenties is the only Christian in his office. When the company announces job cuts, everyone is anxious, him included. Over coffee a colleague says, “You seem less stressed than the rest of us. Why?” He hesitates, then says honestly that he is worried too, but that he believes God is in charge of his future, and that even if he loses this job, he will not lose what matters most. The colleague asks how he can be so sure. They agree to meet again, and he brings a copy of Luke’s Gospel.

For reflection

If someone asked you today for “a reason for the hope that is in you”, what would you say? What does it mean to honour Christ as holy in your heart first? Where do you see the hopelessness of our age most clearly? Who could you ask, gently, what they are hoping for?

12.title: Christ Our Hope
12.essay:
We have spoken of hope as an anchor, a helmet, an inheritance, a city. But in the end the Bible’s hope is not a thing at all. It is a Person. Paul opens one of his letters with four simple words that gather up everything: “Christ Jesus our hope” (1 Timothy 1:1).

Christ Jesus our hope

Paul does not say that Christ gives us hope, though he does. He says Christ is our hope. Everything we hope for is found in him. Forgiveness is in him, because he bore our sins. Peace with God is in him, because he reconciled us. The resurrection is in him, because he is “the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). The new creation is in him, because all things were made through him and for him. Heaven is in him, because heaven is where he is.

Take Christ away, and nothing is left but wishes. Keep Christ, and even if everything else is lost, you have everything that matters.

Christ in you, the hope of glory

Paul tells the Colossians that God has made known a great mystery, “which is Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27). Our hope is not only out ahead of us. It lives within us. By the Holy Spirit, Christ dwells in every believer now, and his presence is the pledge of glory to come.

The One who will meet us at the end walks with us on the way. Paul says elsewhere, “your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:3–4). Our life is hidden with him now. One day it will be revealed with him.

Our blessed hope

Paul calls Christ’s return “our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). The final object of our hope is not an event but an appearing: the moment when the one we have loved without seeing will be seen. Peter writes, “Though you have not seen him, you love him. Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory” (1 Peter 1:8).

The whole story in one face

Step back and see how all the threads of this study come together in him.

We cannot live without hope, because God made us for himself. Our hope is sure because Christ has gone ahead as our forerunner. The hopes that disappoint are good things asked to be saviours; Christ is the Saviour who never disappoints. Our hope is living because he lives. What we wait for is, above all, his face. Our earthly hopes are safe in his hands, our suffering is shared by the Man of Sorrows, and our labour is not in vain because he is risen. The reason for the hope that is in us is, in the end, simply him.

Think of who he is. The eternal Son, through whom the stars were made, became a baby in a borrowed manger. He walked our roads, wept at a friend’s grave, and took our sin and death into his own body on the cross. He rose, bodily and gloriously, as the firstfruits of a new world. He ascended to the Father’s right hand, where he lives to pray for us. And he is coming back. Every longing of the human heart finds its home in him. He is not one hope among many. He is the hope of glory.

Edward Mote’s hymn puts it in words many Christians have sung for nearly two centuries: “My hope is built on nothing less than Jesus’ blood and righteousness.” Not our performance or our feelings, but his blood and his righteousness.

Come, Lord Jesus

The Bible ends with a promise and a prayer. Jesus says, “Surely I am coming soon.” And the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). That is the voice of hope. Not anxious, not resigned, but eager.

If you do not yet know him, this hope is offered to you today. You do not need to earn it. Come to him as you are, confess your need, and trust him. He has never turned away anyone who comes.

An example

An elderly woman in a care home has lost most of her memory. She no longer recognises her daughter some days. But when the visiting minister begins “My hope is built on nothing less”, she joins in, word perfect, and her face changes. Her daughter says, “She’s forgotten almost everything. But she hasn’t forgotten him.” And the minister quietly answers, “More importantly, he hasn’t forgotten her.”

For reflection

What does it mean to you that Christ is not only the giver of hope but hope itself? How does “Christ in you, the hope of glory” change the way you face the future? Which thread of this study has most strengthened your hope? Can you pray, honestly and gladly, “Come, Lord Jesus”?
